StrongBó, an Irish agritech company allows beef producers to collect live data on the weight of their cattle with its hardware-enabled software solution\. How do you get a cow to weigh itself? Put a bucket of food in front of it\! The animal steps up on the platform for a feed, meanwhile the producer gets the data to get an idea of how the animal is growing\.

The Dublin firm, based in NovaUCD has just raised €750,000 in a round led by New Zealand agri solutions firm Gallagher and it also includes funding from Enterprise Ireland via the High Potential Start-up programme and funds from Canada’s 519 Growth Fund and the Grand River Agricultural Society\.

“We are delighted to secure this funding round with such a significant mix of globally recognised industry players and seasoned investors like Enterprise Ireland\. Our latest innovation allows farmers to gain new insights into how their animals are actually progressing\. StrongBó provides average daily gains so farmers can see how much the animals are growing, and how much weight they're putting on\. You can’t manage what you don’t measure,” says Micheál McInerney, co-founder and CEO, StrongBó\.

“Now more than ever, farmers are looking for technologies that enable them to farm more efficiently and profitably\. Being able to regularly weigh livestock while in the paddock can mean real savings in labour output and potentially down the track it may enable them to track the more feed efficient animals and lower greenhouse gas emitters\. Remote weighing also keeps cows on-feed 24/7, allowing them to maximise weight gain, therefore reducing the need and stress from traipsing up to the yard for weighing,\" says Sarah Adams, General Manager of Strategy and New Ventures for Gallagher Animal Management\.

*Main image: StrongBó Agritech co-founders, Micheál McInerney and Marty Metzger, with a StrongBó automatic animal weighing device \(source: StrongBó\)*

BIO-NITROGEN APPROACH: Pivot Bio has created technology that helps corn fix nitrogen\. In 2022, growers can use Proven 40 which can replace up to 40 pounds of synthetic nitrogen in the crop\. The company also announced a new funding round from investors\.Willie Vogt

Ernest Sanders is excited\. \"We've doubled the amount of fertilizer we'll replace,\" says the vice president of product development at Pivot Bio\. \"Proven 40 will enable a grower to reduce up to 40-pounds of synthetic nitrogen in the crop\.\"

Pivot Bio introduced the first commercially available microbial nitrogen product in 2019, and the company says it has replaced synthetic nitrogen on more than 1 million crop acres in 2021 alone\. And with that initial product the company claimed it could replace up to 25 pounds of synthetic nitrogen\. But Sanders explains the company is raising the bar\.

\"We've changed to two new strains that came out of our research pipeline,\" Sanders explains\. \"This is our fourth product launch and we continue to push\. We're all hands on deck to deliver these solutions to growers\.\"

Proven 40, like its predecessor, is applied in furrow at planting with the crop\. \"It has to be in contact with the seed at germination to colonize in the root system,\" Sanders explains\. \"We refer to this as spoon feeding, providing a little nitrogen produced daily to the plant\. It is dependable, consistent, reliable and won't be washed away\.\"

Variable weather in 2021 shows the value of having nitrogen present in this way\. Rains have seen nitrogen leach away from crops\. \"You can count on this being in the roots to deliver,\" Sanders says\.

## Beyond a product innovation

As it announced the launch of Proven 40, Pivot Bio also announced the company closed in $430 million of Series D funding, bringing the total equity raised to more than $600 million\. That money will go to fuel the company's accelerating release of products \"focused on replacing the $60 billion of synthetic nitrogen fertilizer sold each year just to sustain corn, wheat and rice\.\"

Sanders points out that nitrogen-fed crops feed two-thirds of the world's population, yet there are challenges with synthetic nitrogen\. \"Not all of it gets in the plant when we apply it,\" he says\. \"You can lose 40 to 60% by being washed away or volatized off the crop\.\"

He notes there's a lot of research looking at how much nitrogen plants need, \"but a key to that is it does not matter how much you apply, it's what gets in the plant that does any good\.\"

Sanders explains that in 300 research plots in 2020 and in 600 in 2021, tissue analysis is showing that nitrogen is getting into plant tissues with this technology\. \"I get excited talking about it\. This is a new wave of a biosource, not petroleum based nitrogen, that can make a difference for farmers and generate value,\" he says\.

## A different sales approach

Pivot Bio uses a direct-to-farmer selling approach, which differs from other products on the market\. The product was developed in close consultation with farmers\. The company uses nutrient measurement tools, grower engagement programs and a direct-to-farm supply chain\.

In a media statement announcing the latest round of funding, Karsten Temme, Pivot Bio co-founder and CEO, remarks: \"We have built a platform for accelerating nitrogen innovation in the market, and our products are delivering recurring positive outcomes for the growers we serve\.\"

With the latest round of funding, Pivot Bio's next stage of growth will focus on rapidly scaling its U\.S\. business and expanding into key international markets\.

You can learn more about Proven 40 at pivotbio\.com\.

## About the Author

Willie Vogt has been covering agricultural technology for more than 40 years, with most of that time as editorial director for Farm Progress\. He is passionate about helping farmers better understand how technology can help them succeed, when appropriately applied\.

# Agritech Rize Raises $31 Million for Sustainable Rice Farming

Agritech firm Rize has secured $31 million in Series B funding, consisting of $20 million in equity and $11 million in debt\. This capital will help expand sustainable rice farming across Southeast Asia\. Investors should monitor how the company balances its debt-heavy growth with the operational challenges of scaling to 300,000 hectares by 2030\.

Agritech company Rize has raised $31 million in a Series B funding round, bringing its total funding since inception to $47 million\. The latest round is structured as $20 million in equity and $11 million in debt\. The funding was led by BNP Paribas Asset Management Alts with support from The Rockefeller Foundation\. The company aims to use these funds to expand its sustainable rice farming operations across Southeast Asia, moving beyond its current focus in Vietnam and Indonesia\.

### Scaling Operations and Debt Management

Rize plans to use this capital to improve its supply chain traceability and develop new AI tools for field teams and farmers\. A significant portion is also directed toward carbon-certification projects\. While the expansion plan is ambitious, the inclusion of $11 million in debt in the funding mix means the company will have to manage interest obligations while scaling its operations\. Investors often monitor how such debt-led expansion affects future cash flow, especially in the agritech sector where projects can face long gestation periods and execution risks\.

### Impact of Sustainable Farming Techniques

The company promotes the Alternate Wetting and Drying irrigation method to manage water and methane emissions\. According to the International Rice Research Institute, this technique can reduce water usage and methane output without hurting crop yields\. Rize reports that its current efforts have already boosted incomes for its network of approximately 17,000 smallholder farmers\. Since its launch in 2023, the startup has grown its footprint to 50,000 hectares\. The company now faces the challenge of scaling this to 300,000 hectares and 150,000 farmers by 2030, a goal that will require significant operational efficiency and consistent adoption by farmers in new regions\.

### Investor Context and Market Presence

Rize entered the market with strong early backing from global names such as Temasek, Breakthrough Energy Ventures, GenZero, and Wavemaker Impact\. The company has seen significant growth since its Series A round in May 2024\. For investors tracking the sector, the key monitorables will be the actual pace of land acquisition, the ability to maintain the reported 30% increase in farmer incomes as it enters new markets, and its ability to manage the cost of debt while proving the profitability of its AI and carbon-certification tools\. Any delays in scaling the target hectares or challenges in farm-level adoption could impact the company's financial health as it grows\.

# Coffee With Tamer El Raghy on bringing climate-smart agriculture to Egypt

**Acumen****’s climate-focused agriculture fund is coming to Egypt for the first time\.** The Acumen Resilient Agriculture Fund \(ARAF\) — the impact fund known for backing fast-growing African agribusinesses building smallholder farmers’ climate resilience — has secured USD 90 mn in fresh committed capital\. The top-up brings total fund size to roughly USD 148 mn and marks its first expansion beyond East and West Africa into North Africa\. Egypt is one of three new target markets, and ARAF’s pitch here is specific: help move the country’s agriculture from exporting raw crops toward processed, branded goods\.

**The raise is backed by returning anchors and a fresh set of DFIs\.** The Green Climate Fund \(GCF\), FMO and Proparco all topped up existing commitments, joined by new investors Swedfund, BIO and FASA, alongside an undisclosed family office that also backed the first round\.

**Tamer El Raghy \(****LinkedIn****\) has led ARAF from day one\.** The Cairo University-trained engineer holds a PhD in materials engineering from Drexel, an MBA from NYU Stern, and nine patents from an earlier career as an academic and startup founder\. He built his career at Cargill across grain, oilseeds, and animal feed in Africa and the Middle East, before heading agriculture and food private equity in Africa at a Zurich-based fund\. He joined Acumen in November 2018 to launch ARAF and has run it out of Nairobi ever since\.

**We sat down with El Raghy to talk about why climate resilience, not just capital, is what turns African smallholders into lasting agribusinesses**, the Kenyan farmer whose solar-powered irrigation pump changed the trajectory of her farm, and his vision for pushing Egypt up the value chain from raw crops to branded, processed goods\.

**Edited excerpts from our conversation:**

**EnterpriseAM: Your career took you through venture, consulting, and years at Cargill before you landed in impact investing\. What actually pulled you into agrifood?**

**Tamer El Raghy:** It happened almost by accident\. I was an engineer, a professor for four years, then left academia to commercialize some patents, which is how I ended up in an MBA, then M&A consulting\. Then Cargill called, needing someone to run strategy and investments in Africa\. I had no ag experience and no Africa experience, but Cargill is an amazing school\. Traveling the continent, I saw how a smallholder’s life changes when they work with the right company\. That stuck with me because these are the people growing our food, yet they are the most exposed to climate change despite contributing almost nothing to it\. When Acumen approached me about building a fund focused on farmers’ climate resilience, I said yes immediately\.

An impact fund is still seeking risk-adjusted economic returns, like any fund\. The difference is that it also carries an impact thesis it has to report against\. ARAF hires a third party every year, funded through a grant from the Green Climate Fund, to measure how its portfolio companies are affecting smallholder farmers’ climate resilience\.

**EnterpriseAM: Before this round, ARAF had USD 58 mn committed\. What’s actually changing with this expansion, and who’s backing it?**

**TE:** The real shift is geographic\. Before this round, we had USD 58 mn committed in 2021, focused entirely on East Africa and Anglophone West Africa — Nigeria and Ghana\. This additional USD 90 mn lets us keep investing there while expanding into North Africa for the first time\. We’re not just deploying more capital in the same markets — we’re testing whether the model travels somewhere we’ve never operated\.

We have returning investors — GCF, Proparco, and FMO — all of whom topped up their existing commitments, plus new investors Swedfund, BIO, and FASA, and a family office that was also in our first round\. On the numbers that are already public, GCF’s commitment includes USD 30 mn in equity, Proparco is in for USD 12 mn, FMO for USD 12\.5 mn, and Swedfund for USD 12 mn\.

**EnterpriseAM: Why is Egypt only entering the picture now?**

**TE:** We started narrow on purpose, focusing on East Africa and Anglophone West Africa, to prove the model before raising a bigger fund\. Once we decided to double the fund’s size, GCF asked us to name focus countries, and Egypt and Morocco were an obvious choice for North Africa\. For Francophone West Africa, we needed a beachhead, and the Ivory Coast’s agriculture sector is large, structured, and comparable in scale to Egypt’s\.

Not many people realize how big Egypt’s agriculture sector is, or how much of it is still built around smallholder farmers\. We think there’s a long way to go from exporting raw materials to exporting processed goods, and that’s the role we’d like to play\. When we explained North Africa’s potential to our investors, all of them got excited about its scale\. As it stands, we’ll be the first ag-and-food-focused fund in North Africa\.

**EnterpriseAM: Is there a moment that crystallized why this work matters to you?**

**TE:** There’s one Kenyan farmer in particular who comes to mind\. After working domestic jobs in Nairobi for years, she inherited land and returned home to plant corn\. She struggled because corn doesn’t pay well and, without irrigation, a bad rain season can wipe out a harvest\. She got a call about a solar-powered irrigation pump from SunCulture, an ARAF portfolio company\. She ignored it at first, thinking it was a scam, but eventually decided to visit the store\. She couldn’t afford the down payment, so her son, working as a barista in Dubai, sent her the money\. She told us she didn’t know how to write a business plan, so she drew her farm instead — corn to eat, along with coffee, hibiscus, and fish\. Then, she redrew it every single year to track her progress\. Three years later, her farm looked exactly like her drawing, and her mud hut is now a brick house\.

That story is part of why the fund’s own impact data shows more than 80% of farmers working with ARAF’s portfolio companies reporting a rise in income\.

**EnterpriseAM: What does that raw-to-processed shift actually look like in practice?**

**TE:** Take a company like Beyond Good in our current portfolio\. It sources cocoa from smallholders in Madagascar and Uganda and turns it into a fully branded, organic chocolate bar sold entirely in the US\. That’s the model: not just growing and shipping the raw material, but capturing the value that comes from turning it into something branded and exported as a finished product\. That’s exactly the kind of company we’d love to replicate in Egypt\. With this fund, we can wear two hats: venture and private equity, so we’re looking at both early-stage startups and established businesses that could follow that path\.

But none of that happens unless you first fix what’s holding farmers back\. Egyptian farmers face the same four pain points as farmers anywhere across the continent\. First, access to finance, because banks see smallholders as risk rather than customers\. Second, access to the right inputs\. Third, access to markets, since most rely on aggregators rather than selling directly\. And fourth, access to agronomy support — the kind of guidance a US commercial farmer gets from a paid app and satellite data, but a farmer with one or two acres simply doesn’t\.

**EnterpriseAM: There’s a perception that agriculture and food is a hard sector to make money in\. Does that track with what you’ve seen?**

**TE:** It’s not true, and I think it’s part of why the sector has a reputation problem\. People make money in agriculture and food all the time — in Egypt, across Africa, and globally\. What’s true is that it isn’t an easy sector for the faint-hearted\. If you invest in a company making t-shirts, a bad month is a bad month\. If you invest in a company that buys from farmers and there’s a heat wave, yield drops and that ripples straight through the business\. The gap between a resilient farmer and a non-resilient one can be the difference between a good season and losing everything\.

**EnterpriseAM: You run a technical assistance facility alongside the equity fund\. Where does the grant money go?**

**TE:** It’s a grant facility, funded by GCF and other partners, that we manage as a pass-through, separate from the equity fund\. It does three things\. First, it pays for the third-party impact measurement I mentioned\. Second, it funds farmer training on climate-smart practices, including seminars and access to subject-matter experts\. Third, and this is the one our portfolio companies love most, it funds business development support\. If a founder needs an ERP system that costs USD 40k but would rather spend that money hiring salespeople, we might cover 75% of it\. If a company expanding from Egypt into Morocco needs a go-to-market strategist, we pay for the consultant\. And if a promising mid-level manager needs an executive coach, we bring in one of the best, not a “half-cooked” one\.

**EnterpriseAM: Given the water-scarcity and heat-stress outlook for Egyptian agriculture, are climate risk products, like crop ins\., for instance, something you’re actively pursuing?**

**TE:** Egypt’s climate risk is fairly concentrated around temperature rather than rainfall or wind, which actually makes a heat-stress ins\. product more tractable to design\. We already backed a parametric weather-insurance company, IBISA, in our first fund, and we’ll keep looking at crop ins\. We’d love to be part of building that, whether it’s a company already operating in Egypt or one looking to expand there\.

**EnterpriseAM: What does success look like for ARAF’s Egypt bet three years from now?**

**TE:** Three things: that we’re backing good companies with real, measurable impact on smallholder farmers; that ARAF becomes known as the go-to agrifood fund in the region; and that we prove — just as we did in East and West Africa — that the best local talent is already here and we don’t need to import it\. Every member of our team is local\. We like to say we’re an African fund, managed by Africans, out of Africa\.

# Singapore start-up Ropedia raises US$22 mil in pre-Series A round for robot-training data

The robotics data company has raised US$30 million so far, and will use the latest funds to gather more training data, increase device production and expand in Singapore and the US\.

Ropedia, a Singapore start-up that supplies training data for robots and physical artificial intelligence systems, has raised US$22 million \($28\.4 million\) in a pre-Series A funding round\.

It did not identify the investors in the latest round, saying only that it was led by venture firms with experience in AI, deep technology and infrastructure in Southeast Asia\.

The deal brings its total funding to US$30 million\. An earlier round included investors and individuals connected to Google, Andreessen Horowitz, Nvidia and Amazon, according to the company\.

Ropedia's proprietary wearable devices record first-person video, depth, movement and audio as people carry out physical tasks\. The company processes that information into training material for developers seeking to teach robots how to perform tasks in real-world settings\. It offers the data through its Xperience-10M product and customised services\.

\"A robot can't play baseball by watching a video any more than you could learn to ride a bike by reading about it\. The robot must understand what it's like to grip a bat and know the timing it takes to hit a ball\. That's the information Ropedia's technology provides, and it's why this investment matters,\" says Zhaoxi Chen, CEO and co-founder of Ropedia\.

He continues: \"Our technology lets robots capture the experience and real judgment it will take for them to move through the world\. If we get all that right, the robots will leave the beta stage and start doing real work, first in factories, then at home, with families\.\"

According to Ropedia, its approach can reduce data-collection costs by as much as 50 times compared with traditional methods\.

Its wearable device has entered mass production, and the company is already working with more than 20 robotics and foundation-model companies in North America, China and Singapore\.

Ropedia will use the fresh funds to expand data collection in Southeast Asia and North America, increase production of its wearable devices and grow its teams in Singapore and the US\.

It also plans to add tools for annotating and checking data, strengthen its compliance systems and expand research into data foundation models and world models\.

Ropedia was founded in the second half of 2025 by Chen, chief technology officer Fangzhou Hong and chief scientist Ziwei Liu, an associate professor at Nanyang Technological University\.

# Whatnot funding round lifts founders’ wealth as live shopping gains traction in U\.S\.

Live shopping platforms are drawing fresh investor attention as real-time auctions expand across the U\.S\. Whatnot’s latest capital raise values the Los Angeles company at $20 billion and pushes its two co-founders into multibillionaire territory\.

## Highlights

- Whatnot's $545 million funding round boosts its valuation to $20 billion, significantly increasing founders Grant LaFontaine and Logan Head's paper wealth\.
- Bloomberg Billionaires Index reports LaFontaine and Head are now each worth over $2\.8 billion following the latest capital raise\.
- The funding and valuation jump highlight growing momentum for live commerce in the U\.S\. and signal strong investor confidence in interactive mobile auction platforms\.

## Funding round and valuation jump

As reported by Bloomberg, citing Bloomberg Billionaires Index, Whatnot’s latest funding round increases the paper wealth of Chief Executive Officer Grant LaFontaine and Chief Technology Officer Logan Head to more than $2\.8 billion each\. The index is valuing their fortunes for the first time after the company announced on Friday that it raised $545 million\.

The Los Angeles-based e-commerce company says the round values Whatnot at $20 billion\. The funding comes after last week’s raise and reflects investor backing for the app’s fast-paced live auction model\.

## Momentum for live commerce in U\.S\.

# Village Capital deploys $500,000 to three Ghanaian impact startups

The Washington, DC-based accelerator and impact investor made the investments through its $4 millionAfrica Ecosystem Catalysts Facility, a pilot fund backed by **FMO**, the Dutch development bank, and the **Netherlands Enterprise Agency**, or RVO\.

The fund invests in early-stage companies advancing economic mobility and climate resilience in Ghana\. It relies on local ecosystem partners to source, vet, and help select investments while tailoring financing to each business\.

The latest investments went to **Built Financial Technologies**, which provides bookkeeping, payroll, invoicing and loans for small businesses in Ghana, Kenya, and Nigeria; **GrowForMe**, a **Google**– and **United Nations**-backed company that connects smallholder farmers with capital from retail investors, institutions, and the Ghanaian diaspora; and **SAYeTECH**, which manufactures post-harvest equipment that helps African farmers process crops faster\.

“Most traditional financing options available locally are not designed for businesses like ours that are building industrial solutions for agriculture,” said SAYeTECH’s **Theodore Ohene-Botchway**\.  

**Tailored capital **

Village Capital has made five investments since it launched the Africa Ecosystem Catalysts facility in February 2025\. Ghana’s small businesses face an estimated $4\.8 billion financing gap, according to a report by Impact Investing Ghana\. VilCap plans to expand the model to Nigeria and Tanzania\.

The fund invests $75,000 to $500,000 in locally led companies with early revenue and less than $2 million raised, with the aim of helping them reach larger funding rounds\. Its first two investments, announced in May, provided a combined $350,000 to health care startup **Rivia Clinics** and logistics company **VDL Fulfilment **through convertible debt and performance-linked financing\. Built says it has processed more than $1\.5 billion in invoices for small businesses\. GrowForMe says it has financed more than 19,000 farmers, and SAYeTECH says its equipment reaches some 17,000 farmers in Ghana, Nigeria, and Niger\.

# India’s FinTech Rises Globally as Bengaluru Claims Nearly 70% of Total Funding

### **Overview**

- India’s fintech sector raised over $2\.2 billion across 100-plus funding rounds\.

- Late-stage fintechs received more than 70% of total H1 funding\.

- Bengaluru dominated funding, while Accel emerged as the most active investor\.

India’s fintech sector continued to attract strong investor interest in the first half of 2026, even as funding decisions became more selective\. The sector raised more than $2\.2 billion across 100-plus funding rounds, marking the strongest half-year funding performance since H1 2023\.

The latest numbers come as global venture capital remains cautious following the funding peak of 2021\. For India, the H1 2026 performance points to continued investor confidence, but also shows a market where larger, established fintech companies are attracting a greater share of capital\.

India was the world’s third-largest fintech funding market in 2025, behind the United States and the United Kingdom, retaining that position for the second consecutive year\.

## **Larger Fintechs Take the Lead**

The biggest funding round of H1 2026 came from CRED, which raised $900 million\. The transaction was significantly larger than most deals in the market and underlined the growing concentration of capital among established fintech companies\.

More than 70% of the funding raised during the first half of 2026 went to late-stage fintechs\. Companies including CRED, Weaver Services, Juspay, Ecofy Finance and Namdev Finvest were among the beneficiaries\.

The trend reflects a change in investor behavior\. The market is no longer driven mainly by the number of companies raising money\. Investors are putting more emphasis on proven business models, scalability and clearer routes to profitability\.

The same pattern was visible in 2025, when Indian fintech companies raised more than $2 billion, despite a decline in the number of funding rounds\.

## **Lending and Payments Dominate Funding**

Lending was the largest-funded fintech segment in H1 2026, followed by Payments\. Together, the two sectors accounted for more than three-quarters of total funding\.

The dominance of these segments reflects the scale of India’s digital financial services market\. At the same time, investor interest is spreading to other parts of the ecosystem\. Wealthtech was also among the sectors attracting attention during the period\.

India’s fintech industry has expanded significantly beyond digital payments\. Companies now operate across lending, wealth management, insurtech, embedded finance and financial infrastructure, giving investors a wider range of opportunities\.

## **Bengaluru Accounts for Nearly 70% of Funding**

The funding remained heavily concentrated geographically\. Bengaluru accounted for around 70% of total fintech funding in H1 2026, retaining its position as India’s biggest fintech funding hub\. Mumbai was the second-highest funding city\.

Bengaluru’s lead reflects the depth of its startup and technology ecosystem, along with its established investor networks and concentration of fintech companies\. While fintech businesses have expanded across the country, a large share of institutional capital continues to flow through India’s major technology hubs\.

## **Accel Was the Most Active Investor**

Accel was the most active backer in India’s fintech space during H1 2026\. Institutional investors remained the most active investor group overall, while domestic investors participated across multiple financing stages\.

Meanwhile, foreign investors seemed to lean more strongly toward mature fintech firms, especially around the growth stage\. The role of corporate and strategic investors also increased during this period, as they became more active\.

This shifting blend of investors looks like yet another cue that the market is inching toward higher maturity\. More fintech companies are raising capital not only for expansion but also from investors seeking strategic opportunities across financial services and technology\.

## **IPOs and Secondary Deals Add to Activity**

The first half of 2026 also saw activity beyond traditional funding rounds\. Kissht and TurtleMint completed fintech IPOs, taking the number of fintech IPOs during the period to two\.

The sector also recorded the largest secondary transaction of Rs\. 5,352 crore involving Groww\. Secondary transactions, IPOs and acquisitions are becoming an increasingly important part of the fintech funding ecosystem as investors and founders look for liquidity and exit opportunities\.

These transactions also offer a clearer picture of how the industry is maturing\. Capital is no longer entering fintech companies only through early- and growth-stage fundraising\. Public listings and secondary transactions are becoming part of the broader capital cycle\.

## **India’s FinTech Market Enters More Disciplined Phase**

The fintech landscape in India remains one of the most vital destinations for investment across the globe\. The $2\.2 billion-plus invested in more than 100 deals in H1 2026 indicates strong investor interest\.

However, how that money was allocated is what counts\. Over 70% of this investment went to later-stage firms, with Lending and Payments receiving well over three-quarters of the total investment\. Close to 70% of this funding came from Bengaluru alone, while the $900 million raised by CRED was the biggest single deal\.

This trend marks something of a paradigm shift in India’s fintech space\. Investors now seem more selective and are paying closer attention to the basics of the business and its ability to expand steadily\.

The Indian fintech market still has big potential, but the spotlight is probably going to move toward how companies build sustainable operations, instead of trying to raise capital quickly\.
